analysis.one_liner: Sets EPA standards requiring commercial ships to cut fuel carbon intensity to zero by 2040.
analysis.headline: The Clean Shipping Act was introduced in July 2022 with 17 House sponsors and cosponsors, all Democrats, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the EPA to set steadily tighter limits on how much carbon is in the fuel used by large commercial ships on voyages touching U.S. ports, reaching a fully zero-carbon fuel by 2040. It would also require the EPA to set standards eliminating greenhouse gas and air-pollutant emissions from ships sitting at anchor or docked in U.S. waters by 2030. Ships used 30 days or fewer per year would be exempt, and the EPA could soften any deadline it finds not technologically or economically feasible.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in port cities and coastal communities, who breathe the diesel exhaust ships emit at dock and at anchor, plus the general public through lower greenhouse gas emissions. Dockworkers and nearby residents disproportionately include lower-income households, so cutting ship pollution is a health benefit aimed squarely at them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Port city residents and coastal communities

how_it_helps.text: Ships would have to cut the carbon intensity of their fuel 20% by 2027-2029, 45% by 2030-2034, 80% by 2035-2039, and 100% — fully zero-carbon fuel — by 2040 and beyond [S2, S3].

The EPA would have to set standards eliminating greenhouse gas and air pollutant emissions from ships at anchorage or at berth in U.S. waters by January 1, 2030, which would cut diesel exhaust in the ports where people live and work [S2, S3].
Vessels would have to report their fuel use and emissions annually, and the EPA would publish a public report designed to make the data understandable to ordinary readers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ocean shipping lines and cargo carriers, which would have to buy progressively cleaner — and initially more expensive — low-carbon fuels and retrofit or replace vessels, and refiners and suppliers of conventional heavy marine fuel, who would lose their market. Some compliance costs would eventually show up in the price of shipped goods.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shipping lines and marine fuel suppliers

drawbacks.text: Cleaner marine fuels and zero-emission equipment at berth are expensive and not yet widely available at scale, so compliance costs would likely be passed through to consumers in the price of imported and shipped goods [S3].

The bill allows the EPA to weaken each deadline if it finds the required reduction is not technologically or economically feasible, and exempts vessels used 30 days or fewer per year, so the strictest targets are not guaranteed [S3].

Fuel-carbon-intensity rules could shift demand toward biofuels or synthetic fuels whose land, water, and electricity demands raise their own environmental questions, which is why the bill requires the EPA to weigh water quality and waste impacts when judging feasibility [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and climate case is real: cutting ship emissions at berth directly cleans the air in port neighborhoods, and shipping is a large and growing source of greenhouse gases. The honest tradeoff is cost and timing — the technology and fuel supply are not fully ready, costs will leak into consumer prices, and the bill's feasibility carve-outs make its toughest deadlines conditional rather than certain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Lowenthal introduced the bill on July 12, 2022, with Rep. Nanette Barragán as an original cosponsor, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1, S5].
Sixteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].

The action history shows only two entries — introduction and the committee referral — with no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Shipping lines and conventional marine fuel suppliers avoided any new federal fuel-carbon or at-berth emission mandates, and port communities did not get the air-quality protections the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Alan Lowenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Shipping Act of 2022 and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Rep. Nanette Barragán
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction as an original cosponsor; her Long Beach-area district is home to a major port.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral on July 12, 2022.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no partisan split is on the record; all 17 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died in committee without recorded opposition [S1, S4].

industries.note: The bill would force ships on U.S.-connected voyages to buy progressively cleaner fuel, reaching zero-carbon fuel by 2040, and to eliminate emissions at berth by 2030. Compliance would raise operating costs that carriers would partly pass to shippers and consumers.

industries.industry: Petroleum refiners and conventional marine fuel suppliers
industries.note: A carbon-intensity standard that reaches zero by 2040 would phase out the heavy fuel oil that powers most commercial shipping, removing the industry's core marine market.

A guaranteed, escalating demand mandate for low-carbon marine fuels would create a large new market for biofuels and synthetic fuels, whose availability the EPA would have to weigh in judging feasibility.

industries.industry: Port operators and marine electrification suppliers
industries.note: A zero-emission-at-berth requirement by 2030 would drive investment in shore power and port electrification, though ports would face upfront infrastructure costs.
